articles.title: One Risky Crypto Wallet Can Affect an Entire Transaction Chain. Here's Why AML Screening Matters
articles.excerpt: Crypto transactions move fast. A few clicks, a blockchain confirmation, and digital assets arrive in your wallet. For many users, that is the end of the process. But for anyone working with crypto reg…
articles.body: You received USDT. The transaction is confirmed. Everything looks normal. But what if the wallet history tells a different story? Crypto transactions move fast. A few clicks, a blockchain confirmation, and digital assets arrive in your wallet. For many users, that is the end of the process. But for anyone working with crypto regularly, there is another layer worth understanding: AML risk. A wallet does not exist in isolation. Its transaction history may connect it to other addresses, services, and sources of funds. Some of those connections can raise compliance questions long after the original transaction took place. So how does this work, and why should crypto users care? Let's break it down.

articles.title: Can an agent buy from you? A one-cent till, six refusals, and twelve cold agents
articles.excerpt: Most agent-payment demos stop at the happy path: an agent hits an endpoint, gets a 402, signs a payment, gets a 200, the room claps. That demo teaches that a protocol works. It does not teach what bre…
articles.body: Most agent-payment demos stop at the happy path: an agent hits an endpoint, gets a 402 , signs a payment, gets a 200 , the room claps. That demo teaches that a protocol works. It does not teach what breaks, and the thing that breaks is not the payment. It is everything around it. So this repo does three things: A till that sells something small for one cent over x402, with receipts that rebuild from the file on disk. A chaos buyer that runs six refusals over real HTTP, each with a typed code and a fix. An experiment: twelve agents, four doors, one sentence each. What did they read before they paid? The framing: four questions, one protocol An agent that wants to buy from your service is not asking "do you support x402". It is asking four questions, in order: Find.

articles.body: This is a submission for the MLH x DEV Writing Challenge( https://dev.to/mlh-hackathon What I Built Slothpress turns a few words into a typeset quote card you can post anywhere. Type a quote, pick a style, and download a high-resolution 2160 × 2700 PNG. Everything happens completely client-side in your browser tab: no account, no uploads, no servers, and no API keys. What makes Slothpress unique is how it integrates an open-weight model without violating privacy or centralizing control. When you click "Suggest a style", a lightweight, quantized 25 MB MobileBERT checkpoint (Xenova/mobilebert-uncased-mnli) runs directly in your browser tab via transformers.js and ONNX Runtime. It reads your quote, ranks eight typography presets against it, and applies the vibe that fits best.

articles.title: Comparing Batch and Real-Time LLM Inference Economics
articles.excerpt: Batch inference costs 50% less than real-time inference at Anthropic, OpenAI and Google, in exchange for results that can take up to 24 hours. For a workload of one million document classifications a…
articles.body: Batch inference costs 50% less than real-time inference at Anthropic, OpenAI and Google, in exchange for results that can take up to 24 hours. For a workload of one million document classifications a month on a mid-tier model, that is roughly $7,000 a month in real time versus $3,500 in batch, about $42,000 a year saved (illustrative calculation below). The catch is that only work nobody is waiting on can move to batch: enrichment, classification, evaluations, reports, backfills. Anything a user sees live, such as chat, search answers or agents acting in a session, stays real-time. For those, prompt caching is the main cost lever, and at Anthropic its discount stacks with batch. The practical move for most companies is to split their AI traffic in two.

articles.title: I built a malware-triage AI skill — then realized malware could talk it into lying
articles.excerpt: I'm a cybersecurity student, and I wanted to see how well an AI agent could help with the first, tedious step of malware analysis: looking at a suspicious Windows file and deciding whether it's worth…
articles.body: I'm a cybersecurity student, and I wanted to see how well an AI agent could help with the first, tedious step of malware analysis: looking at a suspicious Windows file and deciding whether it's worth a deeper look. So I wired Claude up to read PE files — imports, sections, strings, the usual static-analysis surface. It worked. But somewhere along the way a thought stopped me cold. The problem nobody was talking about A reverse-engineering assistant reads bytes written by an attacker. Every other AI tool I'd seen reads trusted input: your code, your docs, your data. A malware analyst reads the opposite — files whose author is actively hostile and, increasingly, knows an AI will read them. So what stops a malware author from writing this inside the binary?

articles.title: The Taurid meteor shower peaks tonight — and fireballs could steal the show
articles.excerpt: The Taurid meteor shower could spawn dazzling fireballs in the coming weeks! Here's when and where to look.
articles.body: Heads up stargazers! The Taurid meteor shower is upon us, bringing multiple peaks of activity that could see spectacular shooting stars and fireballs brighten November's sky. Here's where and when to look. What is the Taurid meteor shower(s)? Every autumn, Earth plows through streams of debris left behind by Comet Encke, a 3-mile-wide (4.8-kilometer) ice body that orbits the sun once every 3.3 years. These debris streams produce two branches of the Taurid meteor shower : The Southern Taurids, active from Sept. 20 to Nov. 20 and the Northern Taurids, active from Oct. 20 to Dec. 10. As Earth plows through the debris streams, tiny particles slam into our atmosphere at 65,000 miles per hour (104,607 kilometers per hour), producing dazzling streaks of light across the night sky.

articles.title: NASA asks industry for ideas about saving Hubble Space Telescope
articles.excerpt: The Hubble Space Telescope is healthy but is being pulled down toward Earth by atmospheric drag. NASA is considering options to extend the iconic telescope's work.
articles.body: NASA is reviving discussions to rescue the Hubble Space Telescope, which is operating well but is on track to reenter Earth's atmosphere about six years from now. The agency issued a request for information (RFI) on Oct. 29 for "in-space servicing" capabilities, which could include boosting Hubble's orbit (which is naturally degrading due to atmospheric drag), or even a mission to "enhance its capabilities" in some way. Hubble, which launched in April 1990 in partnership with the European Space Agency , was serviced five times by astronauts on space shuttle missions, the most recent being in 2009.

articles.title: Ancient star collisions could explain mysterious Little Red Dots and 'impossible' black holes
articles.excerpt: Collisions between stars in the early universe were common, and this could explain the growth of supermassive black holes and the existence of strange Little Red Dots seen by the James Webb Space Tele…
articles.body: New research suggests that collisions between stars in the early universe were common, which could help explain the rapid growth of supermassive black holes and the existence of strange Little Red Dots seen by the James Webb Space Telescope (JWST). The team behind this research performed simulations of the early universe and found stellar systems were densely packed, leading to stars frequently slamming into each other. While rapid collisions would have destroyed the stars involved, slower collisions would have led to repeated mergers, creating single over-massive stars, which could collapse and form larger-than-usual black holes at the end of their lives. These could be the seeds of the first supermassive black holes.

articles.title: Voting in space: NASA astronauts cast ballots from International Space Station
articles.excerpt: The three Americans currently living off Earth made sure their voices were heard, voting in the midterm election from the International Space Station.
articles.body: The three Americans currently living off Earth just made sure their electoral voices were heard. Anil Menon told us today (Nov. 3) that he and fellow NASA astronauts Luke Delaney and Jessica Watkins voted in the U.S. midterm elections from the International Space Station (ISS). "Yes, you can even vote from space! All three U.S. crew members had the privilege of voting from space station. We filled out an electronic ballot and sent it securely to the election officials," Menon wrote in an X post this morning . Yes, you can even vote from space!
